title: Chiang Rai Night Markets: Best Street Food & What to Eat 2026 | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A street-food guide to Chiang Rai's walking-street markets in Thailand — the Saturday Walking Street, the Sunday Walking Street, and the daily Night Bazaar. Northern dishes to try, real prices, and the best time to go.
keywords: Chiang Rai night market, Chiang Rai walking street, Chiang Rai night bazaar, Chiang Rai street food, northern Thai food
h1:
Chiang Rai Night Markets
What to Eat & Where to Graze
intro: Chiang Rai has more than one night market for eating, and they don't all run on the same day. Come on a Saturday and you get the Saturday Walking Street on Thanalai Road; Sundays belong to the Sunday Walking Street over in the Sankhong Noi neighborhood; and on any other night there's the Night Bazaar near the old bus station that opens every evening. This guide walks you through what you can graze on at each one, which northern dishes are worth seeking out, roughly what things cost, and what time to show up so you don't hit a market where the stalls aren't open yet or the crowds are already shoulder to shoulder.

blocks.html: A lot of people arrive in Chiang Rai and get confused about which "walking street" everyone keeps mentioning, because there really are several and they open on different days. The first thing to know is to check the calendar for whichever night you're in town, then pick the market that matches. That way you won't end up standing on a quiet, empty street wondering where everyone is.

blocks.text: Chiang Rai's night-eating markets — which days they open

items: Kad Chiang Hai Ramluek (Saturday Walking Street) — on Thanalai Road, right in the city center, open Saturday evenings only, roughly 4 PM–10 PM. It's the busiest and longest of the eating markets.

Thanon Khon Muan, Sankhong Noi (Sunday Walking Street) — in the Sankhong Noi neighborhood in front of Wat Chetuphon, open Sunday evenings around 4 PM–10 PM. The vibe is relaxed and community-feeling, with a retro folk-dance area.

Chiang Rai Night Bazaar — next to the old bus station downtown, open every evening around 5 PM–11 PM. It has a food court with yellow tables where you can sit and eat comfortably, perfect for any night that isn't Saturday or Sunday.

blocks.title: Match the day
blocks.html: If you're only in Chiang Rai for one night and it isn't a Saturday or Sunday, just lock in the Night Bazaar — it's open every day. If you happen to land on a Saturday or Sunday, switch to the Kad Chiang Hai or the Sunday Walking Street instead for a bigger, livelier scene.

blocks.text: Dishes worth grazing on at the market

blocks.html: The food at Chiang Rai's markets runs in two lanes: the everyday street food you'll find at any market anywhere, and the local northern dishes worth chasing down specifically because you've made it this far north. We've ordered them by what to hunt for first.

items.name: Khanom jeen nam ngiao
items.blurb: Rice noodles ladled with an orange broth made from tomatoes and dried red kapok flowers — a rounded sour-salty-spicy flavor, eaten with crispy pork rinds and fresh veg. It's a northern dish that's easy to find at the markets and the first thing you should try.

items.name: Khao soi
items.blurb: Egg noodles in a coconut-curry broth made with northern curry paste, topped with crispy fried noodles, with chicken or beef, finished with a squeeze of lime, pickled greens and shallots. Some markets have stalls ladling it into bowls so you can sit and eat right at the tables.

items.name: Sai ua + crispy pork rinds
items.blurb: A grilled herb sausage fragrant with lemongrass and kaffir lime leaf, sliced up and dipped in chili paste, eaten with crunchy pork rinds. Easy finger food you can carry and nibble as you walk.

items.name: Khao kan jin (jin som ngiao)
items.blurb: Rice mixed with pork blood and seasonings, wrapped in banana leaf and steamed, drizzled with fried-garlic oil and topped with fried dried chilies. It's a genuinely local northern dish most tourists walk right past — try one parcel and you'll get hooked.

items.name: Jin nueng nam phrik kha
items.blurb: Tender steamed pork dipped in a punchy galangal chili paste fragrant with galangal and garlic, eaten with steamed veg and sticky rice. A bold northern dish that locals genuinely eat.

items.name: Grilled pork skewers, grilled chicken, sticky rice
items.blurb: Market staples that are easy to find and never miss — skewered and grilled over charcoal, the smell drifting across the whole market. Buy a skewer to snack on or pair it with sticky rice for a proper fill.

items.name: Som tam, yam, larb
items.blurb: The spicy-tangy corner of every market — papaya salad pounded to order, squid yam, mixed-seafood yam. Sit down at the tables with a cold beer and make it a real meal, not just a snack.

items.name: Fried squid eggs and battered skewers
items.blurb: Fried fish balls, battered squid, fried quail eggs — skewered and dipped in sauce, great to carry and nibble while you browse the stalls. Easy on the wallet.

items.name: Mango sticky rice and northern sweets
items.blurb: Finish with something sweet — mango sticky rice drizzled with coconut cream, khanom krok, banana-leaf-wrapped Thai sweets, and coconut ice cream. Plenty of vendors to choose from around the markets.

items.name: Thai iced tea, mountain coffee, fruit smoothies
items.blurb: Chiang Rai is tea-and-mountain-coffee country. Plenty of market stalls serve oolong, milk tea, iced coffee and blended fruit drinks — good for cooling off as you walk.

blocks.title: Bring cash
blocks.html: Most market stalls and food courts deal mainly in cash. Some have a QR code, but not every stall does, so bring plenty of small 20–100 baht notes and you'll move faster. Most dishes fall in the 10–80 baht range per item.

items.name: Kad Chiang Hai Ramluek (Sat)
items.blurb: The biggest and longest, with food, take-home gifts, crafts, and a stage with Lanna performances — folk dancing, fingernail dance, Ngiao dance. Good for a long stroll and soaking up the atmosphere.

items.name: Thanon Khon Muan, Sankhong Noi (Sun)
items.blurb: A relaxed, community feel with lots of locals about, a retro folk-dance area in front of the temple, and plenty of stalls to graze at your own pace — less packed than Saturday.

items.name: Night Bazaar (daily)
items.blurb: A sit-down food court for a proper meal, with live music, open every evening. Best for ordinary nights and anyone who'd rather sit and eat than walk and carry.

blocks.text: What time to go and things to know

items: The sweet spot — show up around 5:30–6:30 PM. Most stalls are open by then but the crowd hasn't peaked, so it's easy to walk and the food hasn't sold out.
Allow 2–3 hours — if you want to eat your way through, catch the performances, and browse the gift stalls too.
Parking — the Saturday/Sunday markets close the street, so you'll park on side streets nearby and walk in. Arrive before early evening and it's easier to find a spot.
Prices for gifts and crafts — food prices are fixed, but you can haggle a bit on crafts and clothing, especially near closing time.

faq.q: Which days is the Chiang Rai walking street open?
faq.a: Kad Chiang Hai Ramluek on Thanalai Road opens Saturday evenings, roughly 4 PM–10 PM. The Sunday Walking Street in the Sankhong Noi neighborhood opens Sunday evenings at similar hours. If you're in town on a night that isn't Saturday or Sunday, head to the Night Bazaar near the bus station, which is open every day.

faq.q: What time should I go to the Chiang Rai walking street?
faq.a: Around 5:30–6:30 PM works best — most stalls are open by then and the crowd hasn't peaked, so it's easy to walk and the food hasn't sold out. Allow 2–3 hours if you want to eat your fill and catch the performances too.

faq.q: Roughly how much does food at the Chiang Rai markets cost?
faq.a: Battered or grilled skewers run about ฿10–25 each, northern dishes like khanom jeen nam ngiao or khao soi are around ฿35–60 a bowl, and one-plate mains or yam and som tam land around ฿40–80. Most stalls take cash, so bring small notes.

faq.q: Which northern dishes should I try at the Chiang Rai night markets?
faq.a: Work your way through khanom jeen nam ngiao, khao soi, sai ua with crispy pork rinds, and the harder-to-find dishes like khao kan jin and jin nueng nam phrik kha. These are genuine northern dishes that taste truer here at the source than anywhere else.

faq.q: How is the Chiang Rai Night Bazaar different from the Saturday Walking Street?
faq.a: The Night Bazaar is a sit-down food court for a proper meal, with live music, open every evening — good for relaxing. The Saturday market is bigger and longer, geared toward walking and grazing, browsing crafts, and watching Lanna performances.
